📖 Core Definitions

Essential Terminology & Concepts

Experimental Studies Key Concept

Experimental studies involve running algorithms on actual computers and measuring their performance.

Asymptotic Analysis Key Concept

It focuses on how the algorithm behaves as the input size approaches infinity.

Simple Justification Techniques Key Concept

To rigorously establish the correctness and efficiency of algorithms, we employ several justification techniques.

📌 Key Takeaways

Section-by-Section Study Breakdown

3.3 Experimental Studies

  • Experimental studies involve running algorithms on actual computers and measuring their performance.
  • This empirical approach provides concrete data about how algorithms behave in practice.
  • The implementation should be as efficient as possible to avoid measuring the overhead of a poor implementation.
  • Step 2: Test Case Generation Create test cases with varying input sizes.

3.4 The Seven Functions Used in This Book

  • In algorithm analysis, we use several fundamental mathematical functions to characterize algorithm complexity.
  • These functions describe how the running time or space requirement grows as the input size increases.
  • Constant Function: f(n) = 1 Definition: The algorithm takes the same time regardless of input size.

3.5 Asymptotic Analysis

  • It focuses on how the algorithm behaves as the input size approaches infinity.
  • Big-O Notation (Upper Bound) Definition: f(n) = O(g(n)) means there exist positive constants c and n such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n .
  • Interpretation: O(g(n)) represents the worst-case scenario - an upper bound on the running time.
  • The algorithm will never take longer than this.

3.6 Simple Justification Techniques

  • To rigorously establish the correctness and efficiency of algorithms, we employ several justification techniques.
  • Initialization (i=1): arr[0:1] has one element, trivially sorted ✓ 2.
  • Maintenance: If arr[0:i] is sorted, we insert arr[i] into the correct position in arr[0:i], maintaining the sorted property ✓ 3.
  • Principle of Mathematical Induction: To prove a statement P(n) is true for all positive integers n: 1.
